interactions.title: Hralgar warns of his dreams and asks for his eyes
lines: DM: Ah, so, at this point, Hralgar begins to speak, gritting his teeth to get the words out. And he says, Be warned: while you travel here, you are wandering through my dreams, and with the ancient power of this place, my dreams can be dangerous indeed. I will strive to maintain control over my mind for as long as I can, but these bonds sap my strength, and I do not know how long I will last.

DM: Sorry. When my connection to the waking world fades and I drift—and I drift as the violence of the storm and the wind, or fade into the pleasant days of trading stories and omens with travelers on my mountain long ago—I will not remember this conversation. It would be safer if you were gone before this happens. And he sort of sighs, and even as he speaks, you can see subtle flashes of sparks and dancing energy that are running across the manacles.
Kenzo: Hralgar, how can we ease your pain?
DM: Find, find my eyes. I can remove these bonds if I could see them. I think this magic is beyond any of you.
Kenzo: Where can we see your eyes?

DM: I do not know. I—my memories are fragmentary. I remember waking up blind in this place. And he’s sort of concentrating, fading in and out of consciousness. I think they must have been taken while I was trapped here.
Kenzo: Do you think Eudomes is behind this?
DM: He pauses for a moment and tries to concentrate. If now is when you say now is, Eudomes has been dead for hundreds and hundreds of years.

before: Seeker: It's like…

interactions.title: Hralgar briefly controls the storm
lines: Seeker: So we better get out of here before he goes unconscious again, or else we’ll be trapped in his, like, dream world.

Delwath: Well, presumably we can escape going back out to the storm, just like we came into his dream world through the storm. But I think the problem is that the—my assumption here is that the lightning creature that tried to kill us was not a bad guy. It was him.
Delwath: ((In-character setup)) Are the sparks and lightning yours?

DM: He closes his eyes for a moment, eyelids fading over the empty sockets, and he takes a few deep breaths. When he does, the mist and fog that lay on the stairs begin to drift away, and you can hear that the wind and thunder outside slow—not disappear, but the noise, the constant dull roar that has been, you know, in your consciousness ever since you cross through the wind wall to the space, fades slightly, and the peals of thunder slow.

DM: And he opens his eyes, and he says, Yes, I can. I can feel the part of me that is lost out there. And he takes a few deep breaths, and he says, I think, I think I can control it while I retain my lucidity, but I do not know how long this will last.
DM: So use what time of safety I can give you wisely.

lines: DM: ((Search mechanics)) So, Delwath, you are, um, like looking through these, these three books. Are they like legends that have been told by elves to their children, or things like that?

DM: Um, so, you recognize there's nothing, at least from the brief skimming you're doing, there's nothing sort of super novel; like you've heard bits and pieces of these before. But what's unusual about these is they seem to be written from the perspective of giants, right, which often is quite conflicting with what you have learned as the sort of received history of the, of the Age of Creation.
DM: But you don't really have a lot of time to read them carefully.

And then the story is—a story will go on for a number of pages written in the Giant script, but then each story ends with usually like with a design. Sort of, not like a drawing of anything, but like abstract art almost, that usually has one or a few runes embedded in the—in the description of the art.

interactions.title: Storm-giant lore and Drankorian marginalia
lines: DM: So, returning back to the library. We're now—so first, Delwath, in the, in the, like 15–20 minutes that you've been reading, focusing on the storm giants, um. So, so this is sort of written in the style of, of like almost like a natural history, like somebody made observations…

DM: These different kinds of giants and, you know, the, the things that you're able to sort of pick up here about storm giants: one is that it is clearly the case that one of the things that, um, that this book describes is the ability of particularly elder, powerful storm giants to transform themselves into physical manifestations of storms and this is partly a way to travel quickly from place to place, but also partly a way to, you know, escape, and to you know, threaten and control people they want to threaten and control. But this is not every storm giant. This is just the more—the most powerful ones, right?

DM: As far as like a way that one would specifically trap giants, there doesn't seem to be—there doesn't seem to be much information about this. This is really much more about it. It's more about sort of giants as seen in the wild, that type of thing, right? So, um, you pick up a few other, you know, a few other bits and pieces of information. So you do find a reference to, to trading omens, in particular that storm giants are, are concerned, among all—more concerned, then, you know, compared to many other giants, about, you know, prophecy and omens and seeing the future and the past. They, in many ways—well, at least, many of them supposedly devote much of their time, or much of their lives, to collecting these omens. Whether this is the sort of human wizards of Hkar sort of speculative writings because you know they're trying to find when the giant kingdoms will be reborn, or what, right? But clearly there's a connection to omens.

DM: Storm giants are also seen as the most powerful and the strongest and, if anything that sort of leaders of all giant kind. So they are, both in their own imagining but also in the imagining of humans and other giants, the sort of pinnacle, the sort of most true expression of giant kind in some sense. You know, whether fire giants agree with that, or stone giants, is a little bit unclear, but they do seem to be notably strong and large compared to other giants.
Delwath: Are there any notes? Like, is there any notes in the margins or anything like that?

DM: Um, yeah, there's the occasional—occasional notes in, in Drankorian, so marginalia of various kinds, but mostly sort of you know, highlighting bits and sort of cryptic you know exclamations, and there's not a lot of—it's clear that somebody has read and studied this book, a Drankorian, but there's not a lot of…

DM: That the part about giants transforming into storms is—clearly has been read many times, and there's pieces of that underlined, and there's, you know, notes in the margin about, you know, Could this be of interest?

DM: Um, yeah. So storm giants, the other—so, the other thing you learned is that storm giants—well, many storm giants prefer the high mountains or other stormy places; other storm giants live under the water. And the two sort of branches of storm giant often look quite different, with the ones living underwater, um, having, you know, less hair and sort of smoother skin and you know, whereas the ones living on top of mountains often with, you know, long hair put up in a topknot, purplish-grey skin.
